Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Thursday, 1 August 2024 at 2pm
(Day 042)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Daniel Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Hilbert Chiu for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good afternoon.
MR MUSTON: Good afternoon. The next witness,
Commissioner, is Dr Andrew Hallahan.
<ANDREW ROBERT HALLAHAN, affirmed: [2.01pm]
<EXAMINATION BY MR MUSTON:
MR MUSTON: Q. Dr Hallahan, could you state your full
name for the record, please?
A. Andrew Robert Hallahan.
Q. You are the executive director medical services and
clinical governance and risk at the Sydney Local Health
District?
A. I am.
Q. That's a role you have held since July 2020?
A. Correct.
Q. You prepared a statement to assist the Inquiry with
its work, dated 6 June 2024?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Do you have a copy of that statement with you?
A. I do.
Q. Have you had an opportunity to read it before giving
your evidence today, by which I mean recently?
A. Yes.
Q. You are comfortable that its contents are true and
correct?
A. Yes.
MR MUSTON: Commissioner, that will be tendered. I think
it's exhibit H5.3, or thereabouts. For the benefit of the
record, it's [MOH.9999.1294.0001].
Q. I think, Doctor, you have prepared a second statement
dated 30 July 2024?
A. That's correct.
Q. Do you have a copy of that statement with you as well?
A. I do.

Q. Again have you had an opportunity to refresh your
memory of that statement, to the extent it needed to be
refreshed, over the last 48 hours?
A. Correct, I have.
Q. You are comfortable that its contents are true and
correct?
A. Yes.
MR MUSTON: That statement will also be tendered,
Commissioner. At least in my folders it is in a separate
folder. I'm not exactly sure where, amongst the folders
that you have available to you --
THE COMMISSIONER: It is where I have put it, so - yes.
MR MUSTON: For the benefit of those who don't have
folders, it is [MOH.0011.0033.0001].
Q. Could I take you to your first statement, Doctor, and
just ask you to turn forward to paragraph 29?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. I think you tell us in that paragraph that part of
your role is consulting with the medical staff councils
across the facilities that operate within the local health
district?
A. Yes, it is.
Q. And in terms of your interactions with those medical
staff councils, at a day-to-day level or in ordinary
circumstances, what is the nature of that interaction?
A. So I'll attend their regular meetings and then if
there are matters which the medical staff council chairs
want to talk about, I'd be available to them for
discussion.
Q. And the Concord medical staff council is one of those
medical staff councils that you have engaged with
throughout your time in the role?
A. Mmm-hmm, yes.
Q. And you have attended periodically the meetings of the
Concord medical staff council?
A. Yes, I believe I've attended the majority of the
meetings that they've had while I've been in the role.

Q. Could I just take you forward to paragraph 30. You
tell us there that the local health district's relationship
with the Concord medical staff council has been challenging
over the past three years?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. You tell us that, at least to your perception, there
are multiple reasons for that?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. What do you think those reasons are?
A. Well, as I outline in my statement, there is
a perception that the Concord medical staff council holds
that Concord hospital is relatively under-resourced and has
been - I think I'd probably say struggling because of that,
and there is also a perception which they've articulated
that the district executive has not been responsive to the
escalations of their concerns.
Q. Those two perceptions, on the part of at least some
members of the Concord medical staff council, are
reasonably longstanding?
A. Yes, they are. So even from the time that I started
in the district, I'd have to say that was a feel of that
staff council meeting, yes.
Q. And in terms of the way in which those or that feel,
as you put it, impacts on staff morale at Concord, have you
observed it to have an impact, or at least to say what is
your view of the staff morale?
A. Overall of staff morale at Concord?
Q. Starting, say, when you first started in the job?
A. I should preface this by noting that when I commenced
in the district in July of 2020, we were in the middle of
a COVID lockdown, so my ability to actually attend and be
at Concord hospital on a regular basis was somewhat
limited. My view, however, is that Concord hospital
actually has a highly engaged clinical staff and morale is
actually generally good.
We have no evidence from, say, the national medical
training survey of junior doctors that we have an issue
with staff morale. There's been no evidence in other
broader surveys of workforce conducted by NSW Health,
including the "People Matters" employee survey, that
there's been disengagement. In fact, Concord hospital and

Sydney Local Health District staff generally have had some
of the highest levels of engagement in the system. So from
where I sat and also from the individuals I dealt with,
I felt I was dealing frequently with a highly engaged group
of clinical staff who wished to make the system better.
Now, look, they weren't - that was not uniform, and
I think that is important to note, that there were a group
of senior medical staff, a significant group of senior
medical staff at Concord hospital, who would not share that
view.
Q. So would it be correct to say, at least at the time
that you have been in the district, that there was an
observable decline in the morale of the staff at Concord
hospital?
A. I would not agree with that.
Q. Would it be correct to say that, at least amongst some
people within the medical workforce at Concord hospital,
there was a feeling of isolation from each other and from
the administration?
A. There is a significant group of senior medical staff
at Concord hospital who would feel that way, that is
correct.
Q. Would it be correct to say that there is at least
a group of the medical workforce at Concord who feel that
the workload and job demands have increased?
A. That has been expressed, though it is not a uniform
thing that has been expressed.
Q. When you say it's not uniform, it's not an isolated
one or two people who have expressed that view?
A. They're not isolated, but it is not all.
Q. It varies from department to department?
A. It does.
Q. Is there a view amongst some medical staff at Concord
hospital that administrative tasks have escalated without
any increase in administrative support?
A. That has been expressed, and I believe is minuted in
some of the medical staff council meetings. Again, I would
suggest that that is not a uniformly held view across all
of Concord hospital, which is not surprising. Concord is
a large tertiary hospital, it has over 350 specialist

medical staff and, you know, thousands, around 2,500 or so
members of staff. So it's not surprising that the views
aren't uniformly held.
Q. Is it correct that amongst the medical staff at
Concord there was at least a group who perceived that they
were not valued, seen or heard?
A. I don't know if that is correct. I - I would find
that difficult to answer broadly, to be honest.
Q. Amongst the medical staff at Concord, was it your
observation that there was a group who perceived that they
had less access to administration to raise issues?
A. Yes. That would be correct.
Q. And was there a group amongst the medical staff at
Concord hospital who were of the view that when issues were
raised, they were not adequately addressed?
A. Yes, that's been very clearly expressed by the current
chair of the Concord staff medical council.
Q. Was there a view amongst at least some members of the
staff at Concord that, were they to speak out about some of
these concerns, they feared that there might be some sort
of retaliation?
A. They had stated that, and that, frankly, has puzzled
me, because to find evidence of retaliation - and we have
asked for that on multiple occasions. That is something
which, in my role, I take extremely seriously and I have
yet to be provided with any evidence that any adverse or
retaliatory action has been taken against a member of
Concord hospital for raising concerns. However, to be
fair, they have stated that.
Q. Is it the case that there are remains a strong culture
in medicine not to speak up and not to make waves for fear
of reprisal or being seen as difficult or as
a troublemaker, do you think? Is that a feature of -
perhaps a unique feature of the medical workforce?
A. I would not fully agree with that statement. There is
actually quite a strong culture of speaking up and of
raising concerns and we have evidence for that, including
in the, you know, current matters that the Concord medical
staff council have raised. I would have to say that my
experience in Sydney Local Health District is that the
senior and junior medical staff are actually quite happy to
raise matters.

Q. You're aware that Dr Cheung, in his capacity as chair
of the medical staff council, sent a letter to the board
dated 12 October 2022, in which a number of the medical
staff council's concerns, at least as he understood them,
were aired?
A. I'm aware that a letter was sent, yes.
Q. At the time of that letter being sent, was it
something which was brought to your attention?
A. It wasn't sent to myself, it was sent to the board, so
I don't recall receiving it personally, but I was aware
that the letter had been sent and my understanding, that it
mirrored some of the concerns that he had put at the time
of his election to the role of chair.
Q. So some of these concerns that we've just stepped
through, which you have accepted were held, not uniformly,
but by groups of people within Concord --
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. -- are things that had been raised at medical staff
council meetings prior to the sending of that letter; is
that the case?
A. Correct. So when Dr Cheung was elected as chair of
the Concord medical staff council, he published I believe
what he called a manifesto, which articulated - from
memory, articulated many of the things that you allude to
in the letter to the board, yes.
Q. To try and summarise those complaints or those
concerns that we've just been through, would it be fair to
say that three of the core issues which seem to lie at the
heart of the concerns being expressed by a body of the
medical workforce at Concord were, first, that the hospital
was under-resourced, perhaps to a greater extent than some
of the other hospitals within the district?
A. That is a core belief that that group of senior
medical staff have.
Q. The second core belief, which might capture a number
of the issues, was that a group of the staff felt they were
not being consulted or listened to by the executive in
relation to decisions being made about the hospital?
A. That was their belief as well, though the basis for
that I have to say I'd question, but that was their belief,
yes

Q. We will come back to that, but a third core belief was
that they felt they were not able to speak up about the
concerns for fear of reprisals and, in particular,
disciplinary action that might be taken against them if
they did?
A. That is what they've stated, and I would also note
that they've spoken up frequently, without reprisal.
Q. Whilst I gather from some of the answers that you've
just given that you are not necessarily convinced that
those, at least the second two of those core concerns, are
concerns that were able to be substantiated, do you have
any reason to think that those concerns were not genuinely
felt by at least a portion of the medical staff at Concord?
A. I completely agree those concerns were genuinely felt.
Q. So they weren't just making it up; they genuinely felt
that that was the position they were in?
A. No, it was actually genuinely felt, and as I think is
recorded, you know, they obviously elected a chair who
genuinely had those concerns and I think at some point in
time in 2023, when a group proposed a vote of no confidence
in the chair, I think 80 per cent, at the time, of the
group attending the meeting had confidence in the chair.
So it was genuinely felt and genuinely a real thing, yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Was it no confidence in the chair
or the chief executive, or both?
A. The meeting was - there were two proposals put. The
first was a proposal of vote of no confidence in the chief
executive, and there was a counter proposal put for a vote
of no confidence in the chair. The vote of no confidence
in the chief executive was carried 60 per cent to
40 per cent, and the vote of no confidence in the chair was
rejected with 80 per cent voting for the chair and
20 per cent voting against the chair.
THE COMMISSIONER: Thanks.
MR MUSTON: We'll come to that, Commissioner.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Perhaps the easiest thing, I'm going to take
the doctor through some of the exhibits to Dr Cheung's
statement. I will give the operator all of the relevant

numbers but to ease us through that process, I might ask
that Dr Hallahan be given a copy of the exhibit, just so we
can all work from the paper.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Q. Which, if you are anything like me, it is
a lot easier.
A. Thank you.
Q. You are, of course, welcome to look at what pops up on
the screen if that better suits your disposition, but --
A. Lovely, thank you.
Q. You will see there are tabs in that folder. Could
I ask you to turn to tab H7.12.8.
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Do you see that's an email that you - just looking at
the first page, which, for the operator is
[SCI.0012.0074.0001], do you see just on that front
page there, that's an email that appears to have been sent
from Dr Cheung to Dr Sammut, Dr Anderson and yourself?
A. Yes.
Q. Could we just perhaps go through to page 3 in the
document to work through it in the reverse order in the way
that one does with emails. Do you see at the very bottom
of page 3 there, there's what seems to be the start of the
email chain, an email of 1 February 2023 from Dr Cheung to
Dr Sammut?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. A little bit has dropped off the bottom of it. I can
show you the rest of it if you need me to, but I'm assuming
that this is what was received by you --
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. -- as part of the chain.
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Do you see there, there's a request by Dr Cheung for
an opportunity to speak at the clinical quality council
meeting?
A. Yes.
Q. You see that in the email?

A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. And a request that some 60 minutes be allocated to
five-minute presentations being given by different people
from different departments at Concord?
A. Yes.
Q. Do you have a familiarity, or did you at the time of
these emails have a familiarity, with what led to this,
what the precursor to this email was?
A. This was really the - stemmed, if I understand it
correctly, from the approach that the Concord medical staff
council had made to the board and then a subsequent
meeting, and I believe the board chair, noting that Winston
Cheung and others had expressed concerns about governance
of the district, had invited him as chair of the medical
staff council to attend the district clinical quality
council, which is our peak safety and quality group, to
understand our governance mechanisms for the district,
because it appeared, as I - and again, I don't really want
to speak for the chair, but it appeared that there was
a concern that the Concord medical staff council felt that
we did not have robust clinical governance mechanisms for
the district, and we felt it was appropriate for them to
attend the peak safety and quality council to get an
understanding of that.
Q. So had you been involved in any of the discussions or
meetings in the lead-up to it being suggested, or that
touched on the suggestion that Dr Cheung might attend this
clinical quality council meeting?
A. No. I believe that actually stemmed from a meeting -
and again, I'm speaking on behalf of others, so please
forgive me if I get it wrong, but I believe that there was
a meeting between --
Q. What we're interested in is what you understood at the
time about the genesis of that. What were you told at the
time about what preceded this?
A. My understanding was that Dr Cheung, as the chair of
the medical staff council, after a meeting with the board
chair, the chief executive and Sr Sammut, was invited to
attend the clinical quality council.
Q. And having received this email, did it appear to you,
reading it from the bottom, to see what the genesis of it
all was, that Dr Cheung was wanting to take the opportunity

to speak to the clinical quality council or have members of
the Concord medical staff address the clinical quality
council about the concerns that they had at Concord?
A. Yes, I understand that and I would also note that this
is entirely different from what the clinical quality
council does. So Dr Cheung asked for - made this request
without actually understanding the normal processes and
structure and use of the clinical quality council meeting.
Q. Well, what Dr Cheung understood about what was going
to happen at the clinical quality council meeting is likely
to have been informed by discussions that initiated the
suggestion that he might wish to attend that meeting?
MR CHIU: I object.
THE WITNESS: I'm sorry, I can't speak to that.
MR MUSTON: That's the answer I wanted.
THE COMMISSIONER: I take it there was some unhappiness
with the question but it may have passed us by, has it?
MR MUSTON: Q. Could I take you forward to the next
email in the chain, an email from - is it Dr Sammut or
Mr Sammut?
A. Dr Sammut.
Q. Dr Sammut to Winston Cheung, Dr Anderson and yourself.
Do you see that?
A. Yes.
Q. The foot of page 2 is where it commences, it seems to
be where you have been brought into the chain?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Had there been any discussions between you, Dr Sammut
and Dr Anderson about this prior to you receiving this
email, that you can recall?
A. No, I cannot recall discussions prior to me receiving
this email.
Q. So looking at that email, after being told that
Dr Sammut is a little bit perplexed, Dr Cheung has been
told that he can attend and view but the opportunity isn't
going to be afforded to have any of the clinicians from
Concord address the concerns they have in the way that

Dr Cheung was hoping might happen?
A. Well, I note that Dr Sammut does propose a way forward
in that email. I think he appropriately - and, you know,
when I saw this email, there was a discussion, but he
appropriately felt that it was very reasonable for the
chair of the Concord medical staff council to understand
how our peak clinical quality council works and have
assurance that we actually have a comprehensive approach to
quality and safety in the district.
He asked that Dr Cheung consider how he would raise
those important clinical issues at Concord hospital he
refers to; he encouraged him to ensure that he had
verifiable data and that if - you know, if that issue
remains and - that there should be an intermediate step of
meeting with Dr Sammut, chief executive and myself, to
further discuss that. So he was proposing what I felt was
actually a very reasonable staged approach.
Q. You'll see, if you track up then to the top of page 2,
Dr Cheung's response where he expresses the view that the
issues have been raised locally and no significant progress
has been made at the local level?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. You would have understood that as a manifestation of
the perception on behalf of Dr Cheung and others within
Concord that they were not being listened to by the
executive, whether that be right or wrong?
A. That was their perception, noting that I and the chief
executive and the general manager had been attending every
one of their meetings, addressing their concerns after
listening to them carefully. But that was their
perception, I agree.
Q. And their perception was informed by their view,
rightly or wrongly, that whilst meetings had been attended
and people had listened, there was very little what they
saw as tangible progress happening?
A. That's what they were saying.
Q. Let's turn over quickly to tab H7.12.9, so the next
one over, which is [SCI.0012.0073.0001]. Do you see on the
face of that, it would seem to be an email from Dr Anderson
to Dr Cheung?
A. Mmm-hmm.

Q. Copied to Dr Sammut and yourself?
A. Yes.
Q. Go over to page 2, you'll see at the very top of that
page there is a response from Dr Anderson:
We will arrange a meeting with you and the
clinicians that you are suggesting with
John, Andrew and myself and they can
present to us.
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Did you attend that meeting, ultimately?
A. Yes, I did.
Q. And at that meeting, concerns of the type which had
been alluded to in the medical staff council meetings that
you had attended were expanded upon by clinicians from
Concord?
A. Yes, there were presentations by, you know, a number
of clinicians from Concord. That is correct.
Q. Again, you had no reason to think, at the time that
you attended that meeting, that the concerns being
expressed by clinicians who attended were not genuinely
held by them?
A. I - I concur, they had a genuine belief that those
concerns were founded and real, though I would note that
they weren't necessarily uniformly shared by all of their
colleagues.
Q. So let's take radiology, for example.
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. When you say that concerns weren't uniformly shared by
all of their colleagues, to the extent that concerns were
expressed at that meeting by a representative of the
radiology department, was it your view that those concerns
were not shared by others within the radiology department?
A. Oh, no, those were shared by others within the
department. So I was thinking of other departments,
frankly. But with respect to radiology, I believe that my
colleague, Associate Professor Ridley, expressed concerns,
which were largely shared by other specialists within the
radiology department.

Q. Can I ask you to go to the second volume in front of
you there?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Go to tab H7.12.60.
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Which is [SCI.0012.0160.0001].
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Are you familiar with that document? It's
headed "Workforce Factsheet CORE Values Behaviours"?
A. Mmm-hmm, yes.
Q. Do you know what the origin of that document is?
A. I beg your pardon?
Q. Do you know what the origin of that document is?
A. I was not involved in the development of this
document. It was published prior to my entry into the
district. It is based on the values of NSW Health and it's
published on the - remains published on our intranet site
in the workforce space. I looked it up yesterday. It
looks like it was published around 2015, I believe, and as
I understand it, remains current.
Q. In its identification of "Below the line behaviour",
just in the first box there, headed "Collaboration", poor
communication is one aspect of the below the line
behaviour?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Disregarding other people's opinions, below the line
behaviour?
A. Yes.
Q. Decision-making without consultation, below the line
behaviour?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Going down to "Openness", the second bullet point
there, ignoring patients or more importantly employees is
below the line behaviour?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Turn over to "Respect", on the second page, just
looking towards the bottom of that box, consistently

agreeing to do something but failing to deliver, without
appropriate communication or feedback, is below the line
behaviour?
A. And your point is?
Q. Do you agree that that's what it says?
A. Yes. I agree it's there.
Q. Showing disrespect for employees is below the line
behaviour?
A. Mmm. I agree.
Q. Contributing to a dysfunctional work environment,
below the line behaviour?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. If we go down to the last one, "Empowerment", do you
see the highlighted section there, "Complain about resource
limitations"?
A. (Witness nods).
Q. Was it your understanding at the time that there was
some concern within the medical workforce at Concord about
how that might operate in the context of the concerns that
they had and their ability to speak out about those
concerns?
A. The first time that this concern was raised to me as
a concern of the medical workforce was in an unfortunate
meeting in 2023 where Dr Cheung raised this document and
effectively yelled at me in an angry voice and shook it on
the screen. So I had not previously been advised that this
was a concern by specialist medical staff at Concord
hospital, to be honest.
Q. In the context of at least a section of the workforce
which genuinely holds those core concerns that you've
agreed they held, could you see why identifying a complaint
about resource limitations and constraints rather than
working, striving to work creatively with available
resources leading and looking into innovative solutions
might be seen as a concern to them if it's below the line
behaviour insofar as they might be wanting to speak out
about what they perceived to be serious problems?
Q. It depends on how you interpret this. So I would
point you to the above the line behaviours on the other
side of that document around making the best use of

available resources to, you know, ensure continuous quality
improvement, to regularly reflect on performance - so
again, it is a balance of things.
Now, I would suggest that I am not aware of
a situation where any action has been taken against
a member of staff because they've pointed out that there's
been a resource constraint. We want to know if there are
resource constraints, however, from the perspective of the
values of the organisation, we want to do that in a
collaborative and constructive fashion, so if there is
a resource constraint we can work together to solve it,
noting that the clinicians actually are the ones who
usually have the best suggestions for solutions because
they're actually doing the work.
Q. But you can see, can't you, the potential for this
document to create concern on the part of a workforce which
feels genuinely that they are seriously under-resourced?
A. I can see how they'd feel like that with this.
I would - I'm challenged by it in that there is a way of
approaching concerns about a document like this, which is
to say, "You've got this document. We find it a bit
challenging. We'd like to work through it. We'd like to
collaborate on it and make it a bit more fit for purpose."
That never happened, and it was raised - this was raised,
actually, in a very confrontational and adversarial manner,
and it was hard to know, you know, really what to do with
that.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. The document would be better,
would you agree, if it had some redrafting on the lines
perhaps you suggested, with some form of explanation that
that bullet point commencing "Complain about resources"
should not be interpreted to mean that staff or senior
clinicians are prevented from raising genuine complaints
about resourcing and that "As management we want to hear
that"? Do you agree with that?
A. Yes, I agree with you. I think documents like this do
need to be put into context and examples of how they are
used do need to be demonstrated.
From the point of view of district executive, my
observation over the last four years is that we've welcomed
staff actually saying, "We have a resource constraint.
We'd like to work with you about it." There are many, many
briefs which have been put up, which I have supported and

endorsed to improve resources and improve resource
allocation.
I would note, when it's said and done, that we do not
live in an unlimited environment, that we do have resource
limitations, and one of our roles, as senior staff,
managers and executive, is to use the public dollar wisely.
Q. A potential problem, though, is it not - and tell me
if you disagree - with a document like this, though, is
that unless there's some education given or explanation
given when it's circulated, that the potential ambiguity or
the two-way meaning of that only becomes apparent when
a problem emerges, and then it's possibly too late, people
have got their backs up, "Oh, there's this problem.
I can't raise it." You're making the point, "Well, we
don't really mean it in absolutely literal terms, that you
can never raise a problem of resourcing", but unless
there's some explanation or some change in the wording,
there's at least the potential of the problem?
A. I can see how that can occur and I completely concur.
Documents like this are a point in time document that
appropriately need to be reconsidered and discussed. They
need to actually be made meaningful and - for those lives
of the people working in the organisation, I completely
concur with that.
THE COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MR MUSTON: Q. Since the angry meeting where the
particular concern about this document was raised, has this
document, to your knowledge, been revisited by the local
health district as to its appropriateness?
A. Not to my knowledge.
Q. After that meeting, did you take any step to, say,
escalate that or suggest to anyone that maybe a revisiting
of that, at least that aspect of the document, might be
worth some thought?
A. I did not take further steps. I was, frankly,
somewhat puzzled as to what was being sought by the chair
of the Concord medical staff council. I really did not
understand what he was looking for.
Q. Well, let's just take it back to those three core
concerns that were held by a group of the medical staff at
Concord. First, that they were under-resourced; second,

that they were not being listened to and action wasn't
being taken in relation to their attempts to deal with that
by the executive; and, third, that they feared reprisals if
they spoke out. You'd agree, wouldn't you, that a group
who had those three genuine beliefs, whether or not you
shared them, would see the identification of any complaint
